 Mystery shows have become a television staple, evolving from traditional police crime-solving procedurals into increasingly ambitious, genre-bending stories. While real-world technology has made remarkable strides, television's crime-solving tools have advanced even faster, often at the expense of realism. There is no image that can’t be zoomed in 100 times but still made perfectly clear.

 NCIS routinely magnifies low-resolution images, to the point where it’s becoming a joke, like when the team found usable evidence in a reflection of a woman’s eye on a security tape. In Apple TV’s Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed , a fact-checker with no tech skills easily finds a clue by zooming in on a screen grab of a video call. 
 Hulu’s newest mystery show finds comedy in the grind of investigative work. Phony is an original mystery series where teen Sonny (Sam Nivola) wakes up from a car accident to discover his mother Ellen (Connie Britton) has been switched with a very convincing imposter — so convincing, almost no one believes him.
 In the second episode, Sonny’s only photo of his real mom is her Costco membership card. When he tries to enlarge it digitally, it just gets blurrier. His friend Mal (Grace Brennan) doesn’t have magic software to clean up the photo, so she tries drawing over it, making it look like a blurry photo in drag makeup.
 It’s a funny inversion of a classic crime procedural trope where, with the push of one button, any photo can magically transform from a few blurry pixels into crystal-clear 4K resolution. Instead of relying on technological shortcuts to move the investigation forward, Phony turns those very obstacles into some of its funniest moments.
 Phony Makes Investigating A Mystery Hilariously Realistic
 Sam Nivola's Sonny looking intently while holding up a Costco card in Phony 
 Before Phony takes a sharp turn into paranoid thriller territory, it establishes Sonny and Ellen's incredibly close, perhaps even codependent, relationship. The transition from family comedy-drama into a psychological mystery is surprisingly seamless, largely because Sonny remains the same sweet, awkward teenager even as his world is turned upside down.

 Posts 
 By  
 Brennan Klein 
 Sonny is hardly an action hero. He's still nursing cuts on his face and a broken arm from the car accident, and he's the kind of thoughtful boyfriend who buys his girlfriend a sex toy before they've even had sex because he's so concerned with her pleasure. He's not someone who would ordinarily make a scene, but the possibility that his mother is in danger pushes him well outside his comfort zone. Making matters worse, almost no one believes there's anything wrong with Ellen.
 Anyone who has ever screamed at their television wondering why a character doesn't simply go to the police will appreciate that Sonny does exactly that. Unfortunately, his insistence that his mother has been replaced by an imposter only makes him appear increasingly unstable.
 Sonny doesn't have a background in technology, investigative training, or even particularly good social skills. When he awkwardly approaches a fellow student rumored to have discovered a dead body, the student immediately assumes he's gathering information for his mother, who happens to be the high school principal.
 These are the kinds of obstacles a conventional mystery series would ordinarily brush aside. Instead, Phony embraces the frustrating realities of amateur detective work. Sonny is just a teenager desperately trying to solve a crime that nobody else agrees has taken place, and his often painfully earnest attempts are all the funnier because they're so grounded.
 Modern Crime Shows Are Basically Near-Future Sci-Fi
 Kirsten Vangsness as Penelope Garcia in Criminal Minds season 18. 
 Modern crime procedurals have become so technologically advanced that they might as well be science fiction, routinely featuring technology capable of identifying suspects through facial recognition almost instantaneously or hacking into virtually any database imaginable. These technological shortcuts have become so commonplace that audiences barely question them, even when they stretch the limits of what's scientifically possible.
 Penelope Garcia's hacking abilities in Criminal Minds are so advanced that they often feel more like a superpower than technological expertise. NCIS has taken technological absurdity even further. In one particularly infamous scene, Abby and McGee try to stop a hacker by typing on the same keyboard at the same time, as though doubling the number of hands could somehow double the keys.
 Audiences don't necessarily want to spend an entire episode watching investigators request access to databases, wait for forensic results, or struggle with blurry surveillance footage. However, decades of increasingly sophisticated fictional technology have conditioned viewers to expect instant answers from computers, even when those answers would be impossible in reality.
 That's what makes Phony such a refreshing change of pace. Rather than giving Sonny access to futuristic tools or conveniently brilliant hackers, the series returns to the basics of investigating a mystery, where gathering evidence is difficult, technology has limitations, and sometimes a blurry photograph is just a blurry photograph.
